title: Parikshit's seven nights
hook: a tired king drapes a dead snake on a silent sage, and a chain of small choices ends in Takshaka's bite
carry: karma is a chain; kshama can break it
tomorrow: the fire is lit. who can stop a king's revenge?

segments.voice: Yesterday, in the Adi Parva: Garuda, the nectar he never tasted, and the bird who became Vishnu's mount. Seva: serve without taking a sip.

A king is out hunting, and he's lost a deer he wounded. He comes on an old sage sitting very still, and asks: did a deer pass this way? The sage says nothing. He's keeping a vow of silence. The king asks again. Nothing. And the king, tired, hungry and stung, lifts a dead snake on the end of his bow and drapes it over the old man's shoulders. Then he rides home. The king is Parikshit, Janamejaya's father. The sage is Shamika. This is how Janamejaya's wound was made.
screen: `A LOST DEER, A SILENT SAGE.` → `A DEAD SNAKE ON HIS SHOULDERS.` → `JANAMEJAYA'S WOUND.`

segments.voice: Shamika doesn't move. He bears it. But his son Shringin, a young man with a hot temper and real power from his austerities, hears about it, and curses the king: within seven nights, Takshaka, king of the snakes, will bite him, and he will die. Now watch the father. Shamika is not pleased. Forgiveness, kshama, is a sage's strength, he tells his son, and the king protects people like us. He sends a disciple to warn Parikshit. The king takes the warning seriously. He builds a palace on a single pillar and fills it with guards and healers. A sage named Kashyapa, who can cure snakebite, sets out to save him. Takshaka meets him on the road and pays him to go home, and Kashyapa turns back. Then snakes come disguised as ascetics, carrying fruit for the king. In one fruit is a tiny insect. As the sun goes down on the seventh day, Parikshit, thinking the danger has passed, picks it up and says, half in jest: let this one bite me. The insect becomes Takshaka, and the king dies. Look at the chain. A sage's silence. A king's insult. A son's curse. A healer paid off. A joke at sunset. Hindus call this karma: every act bears fruit, and the fruit of one act becomes the seed of the next. Many teachers read karma this way, as a web of many people's acts, not one quick verdict on one person. And notice the only one who tried to stop the chain: the old sage, who answered harm with kshama. His son didn't listen. That's the frame Janamejaya stands in, and his fire is the next link.
screen: `A SON'S CURSE: SEVEN NIGHTS.` · `THE FATHER: FORGIVENESS IS STRENGTH.` · `A HEALER PAID TO TURN BACK.` · `TAKSHAKA HIDDEN IN A FRUIT.` · then, large: `KARMA IS A CHAIN; KSHAMA CAN BREAK IT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a small, sharp thing someone did to you lately: a word, a look, a joke at your expense. Notice the next link you'd like to add. Shamika's answer was kshama, forgiveness held as strength, not weakness. Breathe in on the hurt as it is. Breathe out, and let this link be the last one, just for now.
Adi Parva. The opening book, where a king's careless insult and a son's curse end in Takshaka's bite.
Your line: karma is a chain, and kshama can break it. Tomorrow: the fire is lit. who can stop a king's revenge? Day seven hundred two, done.

howItsDone: Vows of silence, mauna, are kept by some Hindu ascetics and by some householders for a day or a season. Parikshit's death is also the setting of the Bhagavata Purana, which tradition says was recited to him in his last days.

fork.setup: someone in your group chat mocks a photo of your family's puja, and it stings. by Shamika's teaching, what's the strong move?
options: don't strike back; say plainly it hurt, and let it end there.
post something sharper; karma will sort out who started it.
say nothing now and hold it against them for months; that's patience.
fork.reveal: Shamika bore the insult, called forgiveness a sage's strength, and even warned the king. kshama isn't pretending nothing happened; it's refusing to add the next link.

chat.meaning: Parikshit's death came down a chain of acts, each bearing fruit. That's karma, and Shamika's kshama, forgiveness, was the one link that tried to stop it.
